Two things follow, and both are the ordinary rules read across the two files rather than anything new:

  • A declaration is in scope in the Pyking half, unqualified and with no import — raw() above is written as any other name of the module is, because it is one.
  • public means the same on either side. raw is not public, so clock.raw() from another module is refused exactly as a def written without public would be. A name declared in one half and defined in the other is refused too: a module offers one thing under one name.

Everything else about such a module — which file implements it for which target, what each Pyking type becomes on the other side, and how the interpreter reaches it — is about compiling rather than about the language, and lives in docs/modules.md.

Modules and types

An imported name has the type the checker gave it where it was written. Nothing is inferred a second time and nothing crosses the boundary but the exported names and their types, so a mistake about one is reported where it is made:

A public function whose type was never written down has the type the checker worked out for it, including its type variables, so a polymorphic function stays polymorphic across the boundary.

tinyweb's implementations, used directly from Python, JavaScript, OCaml, C and Java.

[tinyweb](../tinyweb/) draws, plays and answers on a web page, and every
language a Pyking program compiles to has an implementation of it --
the file Pyking copies beside the program. Each is also a library a
program written in that language can use with no Pyking at all: the
same functions, under the language's own names and types.

| Language | Files | Build |
|---|---|---|
| [Python](./python/) | `tinyweb.py` | `python3 example.py` |
| [JavaScript](./javascript/) | `tinyweb.js` | `node example.js` |
| [OCaml](./ocaml/) | `tinyweb.ml`, `tinyweb.mli` | `ocamlopt -I +unix unix.cmxa tinyweb.mli tinyweb.ml example.ml -o example` |
| [C](./c/) | `tinyweb.c`, `tinyweb.h` | `cc -o example example.c tinyweb.c` |
| [Java](./java/) | `Tinyweb.java` | `javac Tinyweb.java Example.java` |

A program calls `web_init(port)` first, which serves its page and prints
its address; port 0 picks a free one. Everything the program draws or
adds to the page is sent there as a command, and what the reader does
comes back as an event that calls the function the program handed over.
Once the program's own code has finished, it goes on serving the page
until it is stopped. A page that is opened late, or reloaded, is sent
what is on it first.

## What the page and the program say to each other

For anyone writing an implementation of their own: the page the program
serves is `tinyweb_page.html` and `tinyweb_page.js`, which every
implementation carries, and the program answers

| request | answer |
|---|---|
| `GET /` | the page |
| `GET /tinyweb_page.js` | the page's script |
| `GET /commands` | server-sent events, each a JSON array of commands |
| `POST /events` | one event, as JSON |
| `GET /<file>` | a file beside where the program runs, such as a sample |

A command is an object such as `{"op": "circle", "c": 3, "x": 100, "y": 50,
"radius": 30, "color": "#ff0000"}`, and an event one such as
`{"ev": "click", "id": 4, "t": 1.25}`, where `t` is the page's clock.
After each event the program sends `{"op": "event_done"}`, and after a
frame's callbacks `{"op": "frame_done"}`, before which the page asks for
no next frame.

tinyweb used from C, with no Pyking: the library, how to build and run a program, and every function.

tinyweb’s C implementation is a library of its own: a C program can use it to draw on a web page, add buttons, labels and sliders to it, play sounds and answer the reader, with no Pyking anywhere. It is the file Pyking copies beside a program compiled for c23, renamed tinyweb.c, tinyweb.h.

Download tinyweb-c.zip: tinyweb.c, tinyweb.h, the example below, and the samples in tinyweb_assets/.

Running a program

The program serves its own page: web_init starts the server and prints its address, and once the program’s own code has finished it goes on serving the page and calling the functions it handed over until it is stopped (Ctrl-C). Open the address in a browser.

The page asks for a sample beside where the program runs first, then in tinyweb_assets/ there.

An example

Functions

Every function but web_init needs web_init to have been called first, or PYKING_TINYWEB_LOG to be set (below); otherwise it says so and the program ends with status 1.

web_init

Serves the program’s page on port and prints its address, tinyweb: http://127.0.0.1:N/; port 0 picks any free port. Call it before anything else. With PYKING_TINYWEB_LOG set it does nothing.

canvas

A new canvas, width by height pixels, placed below what the page already shows. Answers the number that names it.

fill_canvas

Fills the whole canvas c with color, a CSS color such as "#ff0000" or "red".

draw_circle

A filled circle on the canvas c, centred at (x, y).

draw_rect

A filled rectangle on the canvas c, with its top left corner at (x, y).

draw_line

A straight line on the canvas c, from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2), width pixels wide.

draw_text

words written on the canvas c, with the top left corner of the text at (x, y), size pixels high.

make_button

A button showing title, placed below what the page already shows, which calls on_click each time it is pressed. Answers the number that names it.

label

A line of text, placed below what the page already shows. Answers the number that names it to set_label.

set_label

Replaces the text of the label id with text.

make_slider

A slider from low to high, starting at value, placed below what the page already shows, which calls on_change with each new value it is moved to. Answers the number that names it.

apply_style

Changes the page’s look. With kind “theme”, value names a theme: “light” (the default), “dark”, “plain”, “paper” or “retro”. With kind “page”, “button”, “label”, “slider” or “canvas”, property of every element of that kind becomes value; with kind “element”, only the element id’s. property is one of background, color, border, radius, font, size, padding, gap, accent and width, and value is CSS, such as “#336699” or “12px”. id is 0 except for an element.

load_sample

Starts loading the sound file name and answers a number naming it to play_sample. The name is looked up beside where the program runs first, and then among the samples tinyweb ships in tinyweb_assets/: kick1.wav, snare1.wav, hihat1.wav and piano_c1.wav.

play_sample

Plays the sample sample: at the time at on the page’s clock, or now if that has passed; volume times as loud, and rate times as fast, which raises its pitch as much.

time

The page’s clock, in seconds, as the page last reported it: inside an on_frame callback, the time the frame is for. It is the audio clock once sound has started, so a time read here is a time play_sample can be given.

on_frame

Calls draw before each frame the page shows, with the time the frame is for.

on_mouse

Calls click with the position, in pixels from the top left corner, of every click on the canvas c.

on_key

Calls pressed with the name of every key pressed while the page has the focus: a letter or digit as itself, and otherwise the browser’s name for it, such as “ArrowLeft”, “Enter” or ” ”.

Without a page

Two environment variables, each a file path, run a program with no page at all, which is how it is tested: with PYKING_TINYWEB_LOG set, every command the program would send its page is appended to that file as one line, and once the program’s own code has finished the events PYKING_TINYWEB_EVENTS lists — click ID, slide ID VALUE, frame T, mouse ID X Y, key NAME, one per line — are delivered as if a reader had caused them.

## Running a program

The program serves its own page: `web_init` starts the server and prints its address, and once the program's own code has finished it goes on serving the page and calling the functions it handed over until it is stopped (Ctrl-C). Open the address in a browser.

```sh
ocamlopt -I +unix unix.cmxa tinyweb.mli tinyweb.ml example.ml -o example
./example
```

The page asks for a sample beside where the program runs first, then in `tinyweb_assets/` there.

## An example

```ocaml
(* A canvas, two circles, two samples and buttons that play them, written
   in OCaml against tinyweb.ml. Build it with
     ocamlopt -I +unix unix.cmxa tinyweb.mli tinyweb.ml example.ml -o example
   then run ./example and open the address it prints. *)

let () =
  Tinyweb.web_init 0;
  let kick = Tinyweb.load_sample "kick1.wav" in
  let snare = Tinyweb.load_sample "snare1.wav" in
  let canvas = Tinyweb.canvas 400 200 in
  Tinyweb.draw_circle canvas 100 50 30 "#ff0000";
  Tinyweb.draw_circle canvas 100 50 20 "#000000";
  let presses = ref 0 in
  ignore (Tinyweb.make_button "Play kick" (fun () -> Tinyweb.play_sample kick 0.0 1.0 1.0));
  ignore
    (Tinyweb.make_button "Play snare" (fun () ->
         incr presses;
         Printf.printf "snare, press %d\n" !presses;
         Tinyweb.play_sample snare 0.0 0.5 1.0));
  ignore (Tinyweb.make_button "Does nothing" (fun () -> ()));
  print_endline "built the page"
```

```pyking norun
# Animation kept in time with sound: each frame is drawn for the time
# the page gives it, and each beat is scheduled half a second ahead on
# the same clock, so it sounds where the picture says it is. The
# .events file delivers four frames.

import tinyweb as tw

tw.web_init(0)

c = tw.canvas(200, 100)
kick = tw.load_sample("kick1.wav")
beat = 0.5
var next_beat = 0.0

def draw(t: Float):
    tw.clear(c, "#111111")
    tw.circle(c, int(t * 100.0), 50, 10, "#ffcc00")
    if t >= next_beat:
        print("beat scheduled at " ++ string(next_beat + beat) ++ ", drawn at " ++ string(t))
        tw.play(kick, at = next_beat + beat)
        next_beat := next_beat + beat

tw.on_frame(draw)
print(tw.time())
```

## Running a program

## An example

```python
# A canvas, two circles, two samples and buttons that play them, written
# in Python against tinyweb.py. Run it with `python3 example.py` and open
# the address it prints.

import tinyweb as tw

tw.web_init(0)

kick = tw.load_sample("kick1.wav")
snare = tw.load_sample("snare1.wav")

canvas = tw.canvas(400, 200)
tw.draw_circle(canvas, 100, 50, 30, "#ff0000")
tw.draw_circle(canvas, 100, 50, 20, "#000000")

presses = 0


def play_kick():
    tw.play_sample(kick, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0)


def play_snare():
    global presses
    presses += 1
    print(f"snare, press {presses}")
    tw.play_sample(snare, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0)


tw.make_button("Play kick", play_kick)
tw.make_button("Play snare", play_snare)
tw.make_button("Does nothing", lambda: None)

print("built the page")
```

```pyking norun
# the page gives it, and each beat is scheduled half a second ahead on
# the same clock, so it sounds where the picture says it is. The
```

```python
    digits = s[:at].replace('.', '')
```

tinyweb’s Python implementation is a library of its own: a Python program can use it to draw on a web page, add buttons, labels and sliders to it, play sounds and answer the reader, with no Pyking anywhere. It is the file Pyking copies beside a program compiled for python14, renamed tinyweb.py.

Download tinyweb-python.zip: tinyweb.py, the example below, and the samples in tinyweb_assets/.

Running a program

The program serves its own page: web_init starts the server and prints its address, and once the program’s own code has finished it goes on serving the page and calling the functions it handed over until it is stopped (Ctrl-C). Open the address in a browser.

The page asks for a sample beside where the program runs first, then in tinyweb_assets/ there.

An example

Functions

Every function but web_init needs web_init to have been called first, or PYKING_TINYWEB_LOG to be set (below); otherwise it says so and the program ends with status 1.

web_init

Serves the program’s page on port and prints its address, tinyweb: http://127.0.0.1:N/; port 0 picks any free port. Call it before anything else. With PYKING_TINYWEB_LOG set it does nothing.

canvas

A new canvas, width by height pixels, placed below what the page already shows. Answers the number that names it.

fill_canvas

Fills the whole canvas c with color, a CSS color such as "#ff0000" or "red".

draw_circle

A filled circle on the canvas c, centred at (x, y).

draw_rect

A filled rectangle on the canvas c, with its top left corner at (x, y).

draw_line

A straight line on the canvas c, from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2), width pixels wide.

draw_text

words written on the canvas c, with the top left corner of the text at (x, y), size pixels high.

make_button

A button showing title, placed below what the page already shows, which calls on_click each time it is pressed. Answers the number that names it.

label

A line of text, placed below what the page already shows. Answers the number that names it to set_label.

set_label

Replaces the text of the label id with text.

make_slider

A slider from low to high, starting at value, placed below what the page already shows, which calls on_change with each new value it is moved to. Answers the number that names it.

apply_style

Changes the page’s look. With kind “theme”, value names a theme: “light” (the default), “dark”, “plain”, “paper” or “retro”. With kind “page”, “button”, “label”, “slider” or “canvas”, property of every element of that kind becomes value; with kind “element”, only the element id’s. property is one of background, color, border, radius, font, size, padding, gap, accent and width, and value is CSS, such as “#336699” or “12px”. id is 0 except for an element.

load_sample

Starts loading the sound file name and answers a number naming it to play_sample. The name is looked up beside where the program runs first, and then among the samples tinyweb ships in tinyweb_assets/: kick1.wav, snare1.wav, hihat1.wav and piano_c1.wav.

play_sample

Plays the sample sample: at the time at on the page’s clock, or now if that has passed; volume times as loud, and rate times as fast, which raises its pitch as much.

time

The page’s clock, in seconds, as the page last reported it: inside an on_frame callback, the time the frame is for. It is the audio clock once sound has started, so a time read here is a time play_sample can be given.

on_frame

Calls draw before each frame the page shows, with the time the frame is for.

on_mouse

Calls click with the position, in pixels from the top left corner, of every click on the canvas c.

on_key

Calls pressed with the name of every key pressed while the page has the focus: a letter or digit as itself, and otherwise the browser’s name for it, such as “ArrowLeft”, “Enter” or ” ”.

Without a page

Two environment variables, each a file path, run a program with no page at all, which is how it is tested: with PYKING_TINYWEB_LOG set, every command the program would send its page is appended to that file as one line, and once the program’s own code has finished the events PYKING_TINYWEB_EVENTS lists — click ID, slide ID VALUE, frame T, mouse ID X Y, key NAME, one per line — are delivered as if a reader had caused them.

A short tour of Pyking, with examples you can run.

Pyking reads like Python. This page covers the main places where it
differs. Every example is a whole program: press **▶** to run it, or edit
it first. Each one runs on its own, so a name defined in one example is
not visible in the next.

## Bindings and variables

`=` binds a name to a value, and that binding never changes. A variable
that changes is declared with `var` and updated with `:=`.

```pyking
limit = 10
var total = 0
for i in range(1, limit + 1):
    total := total + i
print("The sum of 1 ..", limit, "is", total)
```

Updating a name that was bound with `=` is a compile-time error. This
example is meant to be refused:

```pyking error
count = 1
count := count + 1
```

## Functions and types

Annotations are optional. Where a function has none, the checker infers
its most general type, so `twice` below works with any function whose
argument and result have the same type.

```pyking
def twice(f, x): f(f(x))
def inc(n): n + 1
def shout(s): s ++ "!"

print(twice(inc, 5))
print(twice(shout, "hey"))
```

A function's value is its last expression, or what it `return`s. A body
of one expression can go on the header's line, as above.

## Control flow

`if` is a statement, and also an expression written
`if c then a else b`. `while` loops while its condition holds.

```pyking
var n = 27
var steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n := if n / 2 * 2 == n then n / 2 else 3 * n + 1
    steps := steps + 1
print("27 reaches 1 in", steps, "steps")
```

`loop` carries values from one turn to the next. Each turn ends with the
next values, and `break` stops the loop. The loop's value is what it
carried last.

```pyking
def factorial(n: Int) -> Int:
    (_, result) = loop k, acc = n, 1:
        if k == 0:
            break
        (k - 1, acc * k)
    return result

print(factorial(10))
```

## Lists, tuples and pattern matching

`match` takes values apart. A list pattern `[first] ++ rest` matches a
non-empty list, and a tuple is taken apart with `=`.

```pyking
def describe(n: Int) -> String:
    match n:
        case 0: "zero"
        case 1: "one"
        case _: "many"

def sum(xs: [Int]) -> Int:
    match xs:
        case []: 0
        case [first] ++ rest: first + sum(rest)

print(describe(0), describe(1), describe(7))
print(sum([1, 2, 3, 4]))

point = (3, 4)
(x, y) = point
print(x * x + y * y)
```

## Recursion

A call in tail position does not use up stack space, so a recursive
function can run for as long as a loop.

```pyking
def count_down(n: Int) -> Int:
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return count_down(n - 1)

print(count_down(1000000))
```

## Modules and the standard library

A program uses a module with `import`. The [standard library](/libraries/)
comes with Pyking. This example reads one line of standard input, which is
filled in above the code:

```stdin
Ada
```

```pyking
import io

name = io.read_line("What is your name? ")
io.write_line("Nice to meet you, " ++ name ++ "!")
```

## Next steps

- Try your own programs in the [playground](/playground/).
- Browse the [libraries](/libraries/).
- `pyk repl` starts an interactive session in a terminal.

The themes a tinyweb page can have, and how to change its buttons, labels, sliders and canvases.

A tinyweb page has a look of its own: the same colors, fonts and buttons
wherever it is shown, whether that is the playground, this page, or the
page a compiled program serves. A program can change that look in three
ways, from the broadest to the narrowest:

- `theme` picks one of tinyweb's ready-made looks for the whole page.
- `page_style`, `button_style`, `label_style`, `slider_style` and
  `canvas_style` change one kind of element, all of them at once.
- `set_style` and `set_colors` change one element.

The narrower one wins: a button given its own colors with `set_colors`
keeps them whatever `button_style` says. Every example below is a whole
program. Press **▶** to run it, and change it to try your own.

## Themes

A page starts in `"light"`. This program shows everything a page can
hold, in that theme:

```pyking
import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.label("The light theme")
c = tw.canvas(220, 60)
tw.circle(c, 30, 30, 20, "orange")
tw.rect(c, 70, 15, 130, 30, "#4caf50")
tw.button("Press me")
tw.slider(0, 100, 40)
```

The same program in each of the other four themes. Call `theme` first,
before anything else changes the look, since a theme replaces what the
`_style` functions changed.

```pyking
import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.theme("dark")
tw.label("The dark theme")
c = tw.canvas(220, 60)
tw.circle(c, 30, 30, 20, "orange")
tw.rect(c, 70, 15, 130, 30, "#4caf50")
tw.button("Press me")
tw.slider(0, 100, 40)
```

`"plain"` uses the browser's own buttons and sliders, on white:

```pyking
import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.theme("plain")
tw.label("The plain theme")
c = tw.canvas(220, 60)
tw.circle(c, 30, 30, 20, "orange")
tw.rect(c, 70, 15, 130, 30, "#4caf50")
tw.button("Press me")
tw.slider(0, 100, 40)
```

`"paper"` is ink on warm paper, with a serif font:

```pyking
import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.theme("paper")
tw.label("The paper theme")
c = tw.canvas(220, 60)
tw.circle(c, 30, 30, 20, "orange")
tw.rect(c, 70, 15, 130, 30, "#4caf50")
tw.button("Press me")
tw.slider(0, 100, 40)
```

`"retro"` is green on black, in a typewriter font:

```pyking
import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.theme("retro")
tw.label("The retro theme")
c = tw.canvas(220, 60)
tw.circle(c, 30, 30, 20, "orange")
tw.rect(c, 70, 15, 130, 30, "#4caf50")
tw.button("Press me")
tw.slider(0, 100, 40)
```

## One kind of element

Each `_style` function changes every element of one kind: those already
on the page and those made after it. Only what is named changes, and
everything else stays as the theme has it.

A color is any CSS color, such as `"red"`, `"#336699"` or
`"rgb(40, 120, 200)"`. A border is a CSS border, such as `"2px solid
navy"`, `"1px dashed gray"` or `"none"`. Sizes, corners, padding and gaps
are whole numbers of pixels. A font is a font name, such as `"Georgia"`,
or one of `"serif"`, `"sans-serif"` and `"monospace"`.

Named arguments are written in the order the function lists its
parameters, and any of them can be left out. The order for each function
is on its own entry in [the tinyweb reference](/libraries/tinyweb/).

```pyking
import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.page_style(background = "#fdf6e3", color = "#586e75", font = "Georgia", size = 17, padding = 16, gap = 14)
tw.button_style(background = "#268bd2", color = "white", border = "none", radius = 16, padding = 9)
tw.label_style(background = "#eee8d5", radius = 6, padding = 8)
tw.slider_style(accent = "#cb4b16", width = 260)
tw.canvas_style(border = "2px solid #93a1a1", radius = 8)
tw.label("Every label looks like this one.")
tw.label("And this one.")
c = tw.canvas(220, 60)
tw.circle(c, 30, 30, 20, "#b58900")
tw.button("Start")
tw.button("Stop")
tw.slider(0, 100, 60)
```

## One element

`set_colors` and `set_style` change one button, label, slider or canvas,
named by the number the function that made it answered. They win over
the theme and over the `_style` functions.

```pyking
import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.button_style(radius = 8, padding = 8)
yes = tw.button("Yes")
no = tw.button("No")
maybe = tw.button("Maybe")
tw.set_colors(yes, color = "white", background = "seagreen")
tw.set_colors(no, color = "white", background = "firebrick")
tw.set_style(maybe, border = "2px dashed orange", font = "monospace")
title = tw.label("A big title")
tw.set_style(title, color = "purple", font = "Georgia", size = 30)
```

```pyking
tw.button("Retro", on_click = to_retro)
tw.slider(0, 10, 5)
```

A small, statically typed, Python-like language that compiles to Python, JavaScript, C, Java and OCaml.
A small, statically typed language that reads like Python and compiles to Python, JavaScript, C, Java and OCaml.

```pyking norun playground
for name in ["Ada", "Grace", "Don"]:
    print("Hello, " ++ name)
```

## What Pyking is

- **Python's syntax, with stricter rules.** Indentation, `def`, `for`,
  `if` and `match` work as they do in Python. A name bound with `=`
  cannot change. A variable that changes is declared with `var` and
  updated with `:=`. Every block is a scope.
- **Statically typed, with types inferred.** Every program is checked
  before it runs. You write types where they help a reader, and the
  checker works out the rest.
- **Compiles to many targets.** `pyk compile` turns one program into
  Python, JavaScript for node or the browser, C89 to C23, Java 8 to 21,
  or OCaml. `pyk` with no command runs the program with the
  interpreter.
- **Comes with an interpreter, a REPL and notebooks.** `pyk repl` starts
  an interactive session. `pyk notebook` serves a Markdown file whose
  code runs in the browser, like the examples on this site.

Install Pyking on macOS, Linux or WSL, with Nix, or run it in Docker.

Pyking is one program, `pyk`, together with its standard library.
Compiling, interpreting and the REPL need nothing else.

## macOS

Install with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh):

```sh
brew install pyking-lang/tap/pyking
```

`brew upgrade pyking` updates it and `brew uninstall pyking` removes it.

## Linux and WSL

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/pyking-lang/pyking-releases/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

This installs the latest release for your user, with no `sudo`: `pyk` goes
in `~/.local/bin/`. Add that directory to your `PATH` if the installer says
it is not there. Run the command again to update. Options go after
`sh -s --`:

```sh
curl -fsSL …/install.sh | sh -s -- --system        # for every user, in /usr/local (sudo)
curl -fsSL …/install.sh | sh -s -- --version 0.2.0 # a given release
curl -fsSL …/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall     # remove it
```

On Debian and Ubuntu, a `.deb` package is also available:

```sh
curl -fLO https://github.com/pyking-lang/pyking-releases/releases/latest/download/pyking_amd64.deb
sudo apt install ./pyking_amd64.deb      # pyking_arm64.deb on ARM
```

## Nix

On Linux and macOS, with flakes enabled:

```sh
nix run github:pyking-lang/pyking-releases -- hello.pyk   # run it without installing
nix profile install github:pyking-lang/pyking-releases    # install pyk
```

`nix profile upgrade pyking-releases` updates it and `nix profile remove
pyking-releases` removes it.

## Docker

The image runs `pyk` in the current directory, which is the container's
`/work`:

```sh
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/pyking-lang/pyking hello.pyk
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/pyking-lang/pyking          # the REPL
```

To use the playground, the notebook or the help, publish the port and
open the link it prints:

```sh
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/pyking-lang/pyking playground --port 8000
```

`ghcr.io/pyking-lang/pyking:full` also holds Python, node, a C compiler, a
JDK and OCaml, so `pyk compile --run` works for every target.

```sh
pyk --version
```

Save this program as `hello.pyk`:

```pyking

```

Then run it with the interpreter, or compile it and run the result:

```sh
pyk hello.pyk                          # run it with the interpreter
pyk compile -t python hello.pyk        # write hello.py
pyk compile -t node --run hello.pyk    # compile to JavaScript and run it with node
```

To start from an example instead, list them and save one in the current
directory:

```sh
pyk example                            # one example per line

```

The playground's Examples menu offers the same ones.

## What else you may need

- `pyk notebook` and `pyk playground` need nothing more: `pyk` serves them
  itself.
- Running compiled output needs that target's own tools: `node` for
  JavaScript, a C compiler for C, a JDK for Java, `ocamlopt` for OCaml and
  `python3` for Python. Compiling alone needs none of them.
- Interpreting a program that has an external module of its own needs the
  OCaml compiler `pyk` was built with. The standard library works without it.

Every read first writes out whatever has been written so far, so a prompt is on screen before the program waits for an answer. ```pyking norun import io ```
## is_eof 
def is_eof() -> Bool
Tells whether standard input has been read to the end. `read_line` answers `""` both for an empty line and at the end of the input, and this is how a program tells the two apart.

Returns

`true` when nothing is left to read, `false` otherwise.

Example

```pyking stdin = "only line\n" import io print(io.is_eof()) print(io.read_line()) print(io.is_eof()) ``` ```stdout visible = true false only line true ```
## read 
def read() -> String
Reads everything left on standard input, from where the last read stopped to the end, line endings included.

Returns

The rest of the input, or `""` when nothing is left.

Example

```pyking stdin = "one\ntwo\n" import io rest = io.read() print(rest == "one\ntwo\n") ``` ```stdout visible = true true ```
## read_line 
def read_line(prompt: String = "") -> String
Writes `prompt`, with no newline, then reads one line of standard input. The line ending is not part of the answer.

Parameters

- `prompt`: what to show before waiting for the line; nothing by default.

Returns

The line, or `""` at the end of the input. Use `is_eof` to tell an empty line from the end.

Example

```pyking stdin = "Ada\n" import io name = io.read_line("Your name: ") print("Hello,", name) ``` ```stdout visible = true Your name: Hello, Ada ```

def write(text: String) -> ()
Writes `text` to standard output exactly as it is, with no newline after it. Use it to build a line from several pieces, and `write_line` or `print` to end it.

Parameters

- `text`: the characters to write.

Example

```pyking import io io.write("one, ") io.write("two") io.write_line(".") ``` ```stdout visible = true one, two. ```

def write_line(text: String) -> ()
Writes `text` to standard output, then a newline. Unlike `print`, it takes exactly one string and writes it as it is.

Parameters

- `text`: the line to write, without its newline.

Example

Numbers: trigonometry in degrees and in radians, powers and logarithms, rounding to an Int, and helpers for drawing and games. Angles are in **degrees**: `sin(90.0)` is `1.0`. Each trigonometric function has a twin ending in `_rad` that works in radians, and `radians` and `degrees` convert between the two. `abs`, `min`, `max`, `clamp`, `sign` and `mod` take two Ints or two Floats and answer the same type; everything else takes and answers Floats, so an Int is passed as `float(n)`. ```pyking norun import math ```

Graphics, widgets and sound on a web page, kept in time with each other.

Graphics, widgets and sound on a web page, kept in time with each other. A program builds its page by calling the functions below: each canvas, button, label and slider goes below the ones before it. A canvas is drawn on with `clear`, `circle`, `rect`, `line` and `text`, in pixels from its top left corner, and a color is a CSS color such as "#ff0000" or "red". A page has a look of its own, the same wherever it is shown: `theme` picks one of tinyweb's, the `_style` functions change every element of one kind, and `set_style` and `set_colors` change one element. A program that handed the page a function -- `on_click`, `on_frame` and the rest -- keeps running after its last line: the page calls the function each time the event happens. Sound and pictures are kept in step by one clock, `time`: a frame is drawn for a time, and `play` can start a sound at one. tinyweb needs a page to show. A program starts with `web_init(port)`, which serves one and prints its address wherever the program runs -- `pyk program.pyk`, the REPL, or any compiled target -- and does nothing in a browser, where the page is there already: on a web page, and beside the program in the notebook and the playground. ```pyking norun import tinyweb ```
## button 
def button(title: String, on_click: () -> () = nothing) -> Int
Adds a button below everything already on the page.

Parameters

- `title`: the text on the button. - `on_click`: the function to call each time it is pressed; by default nothing happens.

Returns

The button's number.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) var count = 0 def pressed(): count := count + 1 print("pressed", count, "times") tw.button("Count", on_click = pressed) ```

    color: String = "",
    border: String = "",
    radius: Int = -1,
    font: String = "",
    size: Int = -1,
    padding: Int = -1,
) -> ()
Changes every button on the page, those made already and those made later. Only what is named changes; the rest stays as the theme has it.

Parameters

- `background`: a CSS color for the button. - `color`: a CSS color for its text. - `border`: a CSS border, such as `"2px solid navy"` or `"none"`. - `radius`: how round its corners are, in pixels. - `font`: a font, such as `"serif"` or `"monospace"`. - `size`: the size of its text, in pixels. - `padding`: the space between its text and its edge, in pixels.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) tw.button_style(background = "#2f6fdd", color = "white", border = "none", radius = 14, padding = 10) tw.button("Start") tw.button("Stop") ```

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) c = tw.canvas(200, 60) tw.rect(c, 10, 10, 180, 40, "teal") ```

def line(
    c: Int,
    x1: Int,
    y1: Int,
    x2: Int,
    y2: Int,
    color: String = "#000000",
    width: Int = 1,
) -> ()
Draws a straight line on the canvas `c`.

Parameters

- `c`: the canvas, as `canvas` answered. - `x1`, `y1`: where the line starts, in pixels. - `x2`, `y2`: where it ends, in pixels. - `color`: a CSS color; black by default. - `width`: how thick it is, in pixels; 1 by default.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) c = tw.canvas(200, 100) tw.line(c, 0, 0, 200, 100) tw.line(c, 0, 100, 200, 0, "red", 4) ```
## load_sample 
def load_sample(name: String) -> Int
Starts loading a sound file, so that `play` can play it without a delay. The file is looked for beside the page first, then among the samples tinyweb ships: `kick1.wav`, `snare1.wav`, `hihat1.wav` and `piano_c1.wav`.

Parameters

- `name`: the file's name, such as `"kick1.wav"`.

Returns

The sample's number, which `play` takes.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) kick = tw.load_sample("kick1.wav") def hit(): tw.play(kick) tw.button("Kick", on_click = hit) ```
## on_frame 
def on_frame(draw: (Float) -> ()) -> ()
Calls `draw` before each frame the page shows, about 60 times a second, with the time the frame is for. This is how a program animates.

Parameters

- `draw`: the function to call; it is given the frame's time in seconds, as `time` reads it.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) c = tw.canvas(200, 60) def draw(t: Float): tw.clear(c) x = int(t * 50.0) - int(t * 50.0) / 200 * 200 tw.circle(c, x, 30, 10, "orange") tw.on_frame(draw) ```
## on_key 
def on_key(pressed: (String) -> ()) -> ()
Calls `pressed` each time a key is pressed while the page has the focus.

Parameters

- `pressed`: the function to call; it is given the key: a letter or digit as itself, and otherwise the browser's name for it, such as `"ArrowLeft"`, `"Enter"` or `" "`.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) shown = tw.label("press a key") def pressed(key: String): tw.set_label(shown, "you pressed " ++ key) tw.on_key(pressed) ```
## on_mouse 
def on_mouse(c: Int, click: (Int, Int) -> ()) -> ()
Calls `click` each time the canvas `c` is clicked, with where the click was.

Parameters

- `c`: the canvas, as `canvas` answered. - `click`: the function to call; it is given `x` and `y` in pixels from the canvas's top left corner.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) c = tw.canvas(200, 100) def click(x: Int, y: Int): tw.circle(c, x, y, 5, "red") tw.on_mouse(c, click) ```
## page_style 
def page_style(
    background: String = "",
    color: String = "",
    font: String = "",
    size: Int = -1,
    padding: Int = -1,
    gap: Int = -1,
) -> ()
Changes the page itself: its background, and the text and spacing everything on it shares. Only what is named changes; the rest stays as the theme has it.

Parameters

- `background`: a CSS color for the page. - `color`: a CSS color for its text. - `font`: a font, such as `"serif"`, `"monospace"` or `"Georgia"`. - `size`: the size of its text, in pixels. - `padding`: the space around everything on it, in pixels. - `gap`: the space between one element and the next, in pixels.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) tw.page_style(background = "#fdf6e3", color = "#586e75", font = "serif", size = 18, gap = 16) tw.label("Solarized, with room to breathe") tw.button("OK") ```
## play 
def play(
    sample: Int,
    at: Float = 0.0,
    volume: Float = 1.0,
    rate: Float = 1.0,
) -> ()
Plays a sample that `load_sample` loaded.

Parameters

- `sample`: the sample's number, as `load_sample` answered. - `at`: when to start, in seconds on the page's clock (see `time`), which counts from when the page started rather than from now: two seconds from now is `at = tw.time() + 2.0`, while `at = 2.0` is already past once the page has been open two seconds. A time already past, such as the default 0.0, means now. - `volume`: how loud, as a multiple of the sample's own volume; 1.0 by default. - `rate`: how fast, as a multiple of normal speed; 2.0 plays it twice as fast and an octave higher. 1.0 by default.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) piano = tw.load_sample("piano_c1.wav") def chord(): start = tw.time() tw.play(piano, at = start) tw.play(piano, at = start + 0.25, rate = 1.25) tw.play(piano, at = start + 0.5, volume = 0.7, rate = 1.5) tw.button("Play", on_click = chord) ```
## play_file 
def play_file(name: String) -> ()
Plays a sound file now, loading it first if nothing has loaded it yet. For a sound played often, `load_sample` once and then `play` is quicker.

Parameters

- `name`: the file's name, such as `"snare1.wav"`; see `load_sample` for where it is looked for.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) def hit(): tw.play_file("snare1.wav") tw.button("Snare", on_click = hit) ```

## theme 
def theme(name: String) -> ()
Gives the whole page one of tinyweb's looks: its colors, fonts, and how buttons, sliders and canvases are drawn. A page starts in `"light"`, which looks the same wherever it is shown. Call it before any of the `_style` functions, since it forgets what they changed. The themes are `"light"`, `"dark"`, `"plain"` (the browser's own buttons and sliders, on white), `"paper"` (ink on warm paper, with a serif font) and `"retro"` (green on black, in a typewriter font). A name that is none of these changes nothing, and says so with `debug`.

Parameters

- `name`: the theme.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) tw.theme("dark") tw.label("A dark page") tw.button("Press me") tw.slider(0, 10, 3) c = tw.canvas(160, 40) tw.circle(c, 20, 20, 12, "orange") ```

Parameters

- `port`: the port to serve on; 0 picks any free one.

Example

```pyking import tinyweb as tw tw.web_init(0) tw.label("The page is ready.") ```

load_sample

def load_sample(name: String) -> Int

Starts loading a sound file, so that play can play it without a delay. The file is looked for beside the page first, then among the samples tinyweb ships: kick1.wav, snare1.wav, hihat1.wav and piano_c1.wav.

Parameters

  • name: the file’s name, such as "kick1.wav".

Returns

The sample’s number, which play takes.

Example

import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)

    tw.play(kick)

on_frame

def on_frame(draw: (Float) -> ()) -> ()

Calls draw before each frame the page shows, about 60 times a second, with the time the frame is for. This is how a program animates.

Parameters

  • draw: the function to call; it is given the frame’s time in seconds, as time reads it.

Example

import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
c = tw.canvas(200, 60)
def draw(t: Float):
    tw.clear(c)
    x = int(t * 50.0) - int(t * 50.0) / 200 * 200
    tw.circle(c, x, 30, 10, "orange")
tw.on_frame(draw)

import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
shown = tw.label("press a key")

play

def play(
    sample: Int,
    at: Float = 0.0,
    volume: Float = 1.0,
    rate: Float = 1.0,
) -> ()

Plays a sample that load_sample loaded.

Parameters

  • sample: the sample’s number, as load_sample answered.
  • at: when to start, in seconds on the page’s clock (see time), which counts from when the page started rather than from now: two seconds from now is at = tw.time() + 2.0, while at = 2.0 is already past once the page has been open two seconds. A time already past, such as the default 0.0, means now.
  • volume: how loud, as a multiple of the sample’s own volume; 1.0 by default.
  • rate: how fast, as a multiple of normal speed; 2.0 plays it twice as fast and an octave higher. 1.0 by default.

Example

import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
piano = tw.load_sample("piano_c1.wav")
def chord():
    start = tw.time()
    tw.play(piano, at = start)
    tw.play(piano, at = start + 0.25, rate = 1.25)
    tw.play(piano, at = start + 0.5, volume = 0.7, rate = 1.5)
tw.button("Play", on_click = chord)

theme

def theme(name: String) -> ()

Gives the whole page one of tinyweb’s looks: its colors, fonts, and how buttons, sliders and canvases are drawn. A page starts in "light", which looks the same wherever it is shown. Call it before any of the _style functions, since it forgets what they changed.

The themes are "light", "dark", "plain" (the browser’s own buttons and sliders, on white), "paper" (ink on warm paper, with a serif font) and "retro" (green on black, in a typewriter font). A name that is none of these changes nothing, and says so with debug.

Parameters

  • name: the theme.

Example

import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.theme("dark")
tw.label("A dark page")
tw.button("Press me")
tw.slider(0, 10, 3)
c = tw.canvas(160, 40)
tw.circle(c, 20, 20, 12, "orange")

Reads the page’s clock. Once sound has started this is the audio clock, so a time read here can be given to play to start a sound exactly then.

web_init

def web_init(port: Int) -> ()

Starts the program’s page. Run as pyk program.pyk or compiled, it serves the page on port and prints the address to open; in a browser, the notebook or the playground the page is already there and it does nothing. Call it before any other tinyweb function.

Parameters

  • port: the port to serve on; 0 picks any free one.

Example

import tinyweb as tw
tw.web_init(0)
tw.label("The page is ready.")

Without Pyking

Each of tinyweb’s implementations is also a library of its own, usable from a program written in that language with no Pyking at all: Python, JavaScript, OCaml, C, Java. tinyweb without Pyking has the overview.
